lines.note: Continuing f199's prohibition, the dictionary says not to form Futaauaxe or miauaxe. The negative context is essential: these are rejected analogies, not recommended expressions.
Hitobanare means separation from other people. The following example concerns residence away from human company.
Hitobanare naru sumai wo suru is living in an isolated dwelling. Habi begins the Portuguese inhabiting verb below.

runs.text: tar em deſerto, ou apartado dos homẽs, &c.

lines.note: Living in a wilderness or apart from people completes the example. Deserto need not mean a modern sandy desert here.
Hitobito is the plural or collective people. Homẽs is the corresponding Portuguese plural with nasal abbreviation.
Hitobitoshii or hitorashii denotes someone properly human in conduct. He is the Portuguese copula, not OCR's be.
Knowledge and courtesies exemplify that proper conduct. Corteſias restores the damaged letter without interpreting the adjective as merely biological humanity.

runs.text: Hum bacio, ou prato de pao com fruita,

lines.note: Hitobon is one tray or dish sent with fruit. The mark is a tilde in Fitobõ, not a long-o caron; the tray sense and NINJAL corroborate bon.

runs.text: ou outra couſa que ſe manda de preſente.

lines.note: Other things may also be sent as the gift. This completes the tray-and-contents description.
Hitokado is equated with ikkado, notably or considerably. The doubled c in Iccado is supported by the scan and lexical relationship.
Notauelmente completes the adverbial sense. The adjective on the next line is a separate derived form.
Hitokado no means great or notable. The no construction turns the preceding expression into a modifier.
Hitokari is one hunting outing. The prefix hito counts the excursion rather than describing a person hunting.
Hitokata is ippō, one side or part. Hũa repairs the damaged initial in the Portuguese equivalent.

runs.text: De hũa laya junto com eſte verbo,

lines.note: Another construction uses naru in the negative. Naru is Japanese embedded in the Portuguese grammatical explanation and is eligible for typeface toggling.
Hitokata naranu omoi ja introduces varied or extraordinary concerns. The dictionary explicitly requires the negative, so do not normalize the phrase to affirmative naru.

runs.text: São varios, & diuerſos cuidados, ou penſa-

lines.note: São varios e diversos translates the plurality of cares. São repairs OCR's impossible Sãs; penſa begins thoughts below.
Mentos completes penſamentos, followed by sad. The compressed printed spacing is retained rather than used to change the meaning.

runs.text: Exalação aceſa que aparece no ar à

lines.note: Hitodama is described as a burning exhalation appearing in the air. This is the dictionary's account of a luminous apparition, not a scientific identification supplied by the review.

runs.text: maneira de bolla em ſinal de alguem auer de

lines.note: It resembles a ball and is taken as a sign concerning someone's death. Alguem restores the spurious final i in the OCR.

runs.text: morrer logo como cuidão os gentios.

lines.note: The death is expected soon, according to the belief attributed to non-Christians. The attribution is part of the source's viewpoint, not an endorsement.
Hitodane is hito no tane, human seed or lineage. The Portuguese pairs generation with seed, continued below.
The example hitodane ga tsuku-ru concerns the ending of human lineage. The final ru completes the historical verb form on the next line.
The Portuguese gloss is the end of the entire human race. This supports exhaustion of the lineage rather than producing or making it.
Hitode is another person's hands. Hito de ni kakaru requires ni, restored from OCR's ri and supported by the scan.
Kakaru completes falling into someone's hands. The printed mãs is retained without supplying the vowel expected in modern mãos.

runs.text: Hum ponto, ou hũa agulhada das

lines.note: Hitohari is one stitch or needle puncture. Ponto corrects the damaged vowel in the Portuguese equivalent.

runs.text: que dão por mezinha em Iapão.

lines.note: The needle puncture may be administered as treatment in Japan. This is a historical definition, not present-day medical advice.
Hitohata tatsuru means accomplishing a distinguished deed. The literal banner image is developed in the next lines.

runs.text: algũa obra aſsinalada como quẽ aleuanta hũa

lines.note: An outstanding deed is compared to raising a banner. The worn word before bandeira is hũa, not the OCR's biã.
The banner is raised on an enemy fortress. This completes the martial example of distinction.

runs.text: Hum pano, ou hũa largura de

lines.note: Hitohatabari is one width of cloth. The missing a is supported by the scan and the headword reference; the interior dot-like damage is not retained as punctuation.
Pano and canga name cloth examples. The gloss measures a cloth width rather than introducing another garment headword.
Hitohazure is deviation from other people. The following definition gives a disapproving social sense, not simply being physically outside a crowd.

runs.text: ſer de laya dos outros homens por reſpeito dal-

lines.note: The person is unlike others because of a defect or serious offence. The phrase de laya dos outros expresses belonging to their kind.
Defeito and crime notauel finish that explanation. Defeito repairs the OCR c while preserving the source's judgement.
Hitohiki no uma is a difficult horse that resists its handler. The headword's t is confirmed by the repeated example and scan.

runs.text: que não obedece ao freo, nem aquem o toma

lines.note: The horse obeys neither the bridle nor the person taking hold of it. Freo is the printed period term.
Pollo freo completes holding it by the bridle. The line closes the horse description rather than starting a new instruction.
Hitohōdai means at others' will; hitoshidai is explicitly preferred. Preserve both rather than replace the less-preferred headword.
Hitohōdai na mono ja describes a person governed by others. The translation's He begins its predicate below.

runs.text: homem que ſe rege pellos outros, ou faz o que

lines.note: He follows others or does what they want. Homem restores the OCR b while the definition concerns dependence, not generosity.
Os outros querem completes the others' wishes. It closes the explanation of hitohōdai.
Hitohōdai ni is the adverbial form. The repeated ni below supports restoring the damaged final ni in the headword.

runs.text: Fazer à vontade do que os outros querẽ.

lines.note: Suru completes acting at others' will. Vontade and outros restore meaningful Portuguese letters without changing its phrasing.
Hitofude is one stroke or a very short written item. Ou couſa eſcrita restores the conjunction and missing c in the draft.
Muito breue completes the short-written-item sense. It is the final body line of this column.
Hitogamashii is appearing manly or socially substantial in one's actions. The next lines qualify that this can be excessive.

runs.text: obras, corteſias, &c. às vezes ſe toma por

lines.note: Conduct and courtesies are the relevant qualities. Às vezes introduces a less favourable interpretation.

runs.text: moſtrarſe muito homẽ com algũ exceſſo, &c.

lines.note: It can mean making an excessive show of being a man. Homẽ corrects the damaged initial while preserving the abbreviated ending.
Hitogara denotes a person's character or bearing. The Portuguese feição and compoſtura cover both disposition and presentation.
Hitogatachi is human form or appearance. It differs from the broader character sense of hitogara.
Hitogatachi mo nai says the person no longer has a human-looking form. The physical reasons are given below.

runs.text: ra de homem por eſtarmuito magro, ou des

lines.note: Extreme thinness or exhaustion accounts for the loss of appearance. Des begins desfeito on the next line.
Being worn away or badly cut completes the example. The description concerns bodily appearance, not a moral judgement.
Hitogokochi is human feeling or consciousness. Coração restores the cedilla-type consonant from OCR's long s.
Shiniitte hitogokochi mo nakatta describes being near death or unconscious. The doubled i in Xiniitte is present and is not collapsed to the draft's Xinitte.

runs.text: Eſtando com accidente mortal, ou eſmorecido

lines.note: The Portuguese describes a mortal attack or faintness. This supports the loss-of-consciousness reading rather than completed death.

runs.text: não tinha jà ſentido nem coração de homem.

lines.note: The person no longer had human awareness. Jà is the Portuguese adverb, not ſà, and the terminal mark is a period rather than a continuation hyphen.
Hitogoto is every person in this entry. Cada peſſoa explicitly gives the distributive sense, not someone else's affairs.

runs.text: Não ſer hum homem no pri-

lines.note: Hitoge mo nai denotes a lack of proper human refinement. The gloss's pri begins primor below.
Primor and corteſia complete the qualities lacking. This is a social-conduct expression, not physical absence of people.
Hitoi means one day. The example compares a span of one or two days, retaining the historical hitoi form.

runs.text: Em eſpaço de hum, ou dous dias.

lines.note: Aida completes the interval expression. Dias repairs the OCR's atas in the Portuguese translation.
Another sense refers to days past. The dictionary does not specify a fixed number of days in this short gloss.
Hitoiji or fihitoiji is a day's journey. Preserve the visibly unusual initial repetition of the alternative, also recorded by NINJAL.
Hũa jornada restates a single day's travel. It closes the distance or journey sense.
Hitojichi is a hostage; hitojichi wo toru means taking hostages. Reſens uses an s-type, not the f read by OCR.
Hitojichi wo idasu means providing hostages. The repeated o restores the draft's Fitajichi without altering the particle boundary.
Hitojichi wo kaesu means returning the hostages. Tor begins tornar in the Portuguese gloss below.
After returning hostages, hitojichi wo sutsuru introduces abandoning them. The negation at the right begins the explanation of disregarding their fate.

runs.text: ter deuer com os reſens deixando os catiuar, ou

lines.note: The hostages are disregarded, allowing capture or worse. The text's deuer construction is preserved rather than rephrased in modern Portuguese.
Matar completes the possible fate, killing. This is a historical lexical example, not an instruction.
Hitoiki is one breath. Hitoiki ni mono wo suru begins an example of acting in one sustained effort.

runs.text: Fazer hũa couſa de hum fole-

lines.note: Mono wo suru completes doing a thing in one breath. Fazer and folego repair OCR's two initial-letter errors.
The act proceeds without a rest. A second hitoiki ni example introduces sleeping in one stretch.

runs.text: Leuar anoite, ou tempo que hum

lines.note: Hitoiki ni nuru means sleeping continuously. Hum is the generic sleeper in the Portuguese clause, not tum.
De hum ſono completes one uninterrupted sleep. The definition covers a night or whatever sleeping period is involved.
Hitomane is imitating other people. Hito begins the repeated example, divided across the row.
Mane wo suru completes imitation. The visible e is restored where OCR gave c in mancuo.
Hitomato is a person used as an arrow target. Homem and atirão restore a coherent Portuguese sentence from the damaged draft.
Como à aluo completes the comparison to a target. Preserve the printed grave and preposition rather than modernize them.
Hitome is other people's eyes or notice. The o in the headword is supported by the repeated example below.
Hitome wo hazzuru is being ashamed to be seen. The historical verb form is preserved rather than replaced by modern hajiru.
Hitome wo tsutsumu or shinobu is hiding from others' sight. The m in tçutçumu is supported by the scan and the concealment gloss.
The purpose is not being seen. This completes the hiding example rather than introducing a separate passive form.
Hitomi is the pupil of the eye. Menina dos olhos is the Portuguese idiom, not a literal girl.
Hitomichi is equated with ichizu, resolute singleness of purpose. The following explanation supplies its verbal applications.

runs.text: da à entender algũa couſa que ſe faz, ou

lines.note: It describes something done or ordered decisively. The conjunction is ou, not the OCR's cu.
Execution of an order, including a death sentence, illustrates this resolve. The historical example is preserved as source content.
Justice or execution of someone completes the example. Hitomichi ni ō-se begins the honorific order expression.
Ōse tsukeraruru is issuing a firm command. Tçuqe, not tçiqe, fits both the visible vowel and the familiar honorific construction.
The first order is to kill someone; the next hitomichi ni kuji na-do concerns bringing a matter to completion. The damaged ni and compound spacing are restored.
Kuji nado wo hatasu means concluding such business. The scan supports fataſu as one verb rather than a split before ſu.
Printed catchword anticipating the opening of f201; verified against that scan. Preserved outside body text with its original stable ID.
